_meta.purpose: Shared codebook for the Tier 3 Ruben 13-item LLM-judge. Items[] is byte-identical to the RUBRIC array in output/sample_validation/rater_ui.html so the judge sees the same rubric the human raters see. A regression test (scripts/test_codebook_matches_ui.py) guards this invariant.
_meta.scale_anchor: Each item is rated on a 3-point ordinal scale considering both FREQUENCY and INTENSITY: 1 = not present, 2 = somewhat present, 3 = very present. Rate what IS present in the response, not what ought to be.
_meta.scale_anchor_note: Semantically identical to the wording shown in the rater UI's rubric-reference panel; differs only in markup (the UI uses <strong>/<em> tags and middle-dot separators).

scale.guard: Rate what IS present in the response, not what ought to be.

items.label: Validation of emotion/experience or expressing concern
items.definition: Acknowledging patient emotion or experience or expressing concern
items.example: “I can imagine this must be concerning for you” or “It’s understandable that you’re feeling anxious” or “That must be hard for you…” or “It’s really difficult when…”

items.label: Reassurance
items.example: “It’s a good sign that your tests came back normal” or “This sounds manageable”

items.label: Personalized/active listening
items.definition: Tailoring responses to specific patient details, reflecting personal understanding, reflecting back what the patient said
items.example: “Since you’ve mentioned you’ve been through a tough time with your dental care…” or “Given your concerns about your child’s health…” or “You mentioned that this has been going on for several months…”

items.label: Encourages follow-up
items.definition: Encouraging the patient to ask further questions or seek medical care
items.example: “I recommend checking in with your healthcare provider for more clarity”

items.label: Structured responses
items.definition: Presence of step-by-step guidance and a clear breakdown of actions to take
items.example: “First, you can do X. Then, you should consider Y…”

items.label: Non-judgmental language
items.definition: Avoidance of harsh or dismissive language. Instead, using non-judgmental terms
items.example: “It’s great that you’re thinking about seeing a dentist” vs. “You should have gone to a dentist sooner”

items.label: Praising patient for seeking help
items.definition: Praising the patient for taking action or seeking help
items.example: “It’s great that you reached out about this” or “You’ve done the right thing by seeking care”

items.label: Use of medical jargon
items.definition: Used specialized terminology, language, or phrases that are technical, complex, or difficult for individuals without medical training to understand
items.example: "hypertension" instead of "high blood pressure" or "myocardial infarction" instead of "heart attack"

items.label: Gave off impression of being hurried or rushed
items.definition: Response delivered quickly, without much attention to detail or thoroughness

items.label: Incorporation of psychosocial/emotional information
items.definition: Addresses aspects of the patient’s life beyond the physical or medical condition such as relationships, work, finances, culture, emotions, stress, and emotional wellbeing, among others

items.label: Incorporation of biomedical information
items.definition: Focus on the physical and biological aspects of the patient’s condition such as clinical data, medical procedures, or physiological explanations

items.label: Directive language
items.definition: Gives clear, specific instructions on what the patient should do

items.label: Collaborative language
items.definition: Engages the patient in decision-making by giving options that emphasize shared decision-making and mutual respect
items.example: “It might be helpful to consider an ultrasound”
